summary: Extends iCalendar (RFC 5545) so recurring events can follow calendars other than the Gregorian one, such as lunar or other regional calendars. It also describes how CalDAV servers and clients can support these recurrence rules.

plainLanguage.summary: Some holidays follow different calendars than the one on your wall. This lets calendar programs repeat events by those other calendars, so a festival lands on the right day each year.

questions: how do i repeat an event on the chinese calendar
what does skip=forward do in rrule
subtitle: Lets a repeating calendar event follow the Chinese, Hebrew, Ethiopic or another calendar, while the file itself stays Gregorian.

tldr.problem: iCalendar can only express recurring events in Gregorian terms, yet many anniversaries and local, religious or civil holidays follow other calendars. The existing CALSCALE property was never used and applies to a whole calendar object.
tldr.mechanism: The RRULE property gains an RSCALE element naming a calendar system and a SKIP element for dates that do not exist in a given year, and month numbers may carry an L suffix for leap months. Dates in the file remain Gregorian.
tldr.outcome: Calendar software converts the start date into the named calendar, steps through the rule there, and converts each instance back to Gregorian. The RFC also defines how this works with iTIP, xCal, jCal and CalDAV.

today: RFC 7529 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2015 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It updates RFC 5545, RFC 6321 and RFC 7265 by extending their RRULE definitions.

sections.title: Why Non-Gregorian Recurrence
sections.content:
iCalendar (RFC 5545) represents dates and times using the Gregorian calendar only. It does have a CALSCALE property for other calendars, but the RFC notes this has never been used. Yet there is a need for non-Gregorian recurrence patterns to cover anniversaries and many local, religious or civil holidays.

The RFC names two problems with CALSCALE. It sits on the top-level VCALENDAR object, so it applies to everything inside and would prevent mixing, for example, the Gregorian New Year and Chinese New Year in one object. And time zone rules are published in Gregorian terms and stored in VTIMEZONE components, so a VTIMEZONE is fixed to Gregorian while a VEVENT may want something else.

The solution keeps CALSCALE at Gregorian and instead extends the RRULE recurrence property. All DATE, DATE-TIME and PERIOD values stay Gregorian, and calendar user agents and servers map between calendars to expand the instances. The RFC does not define calendar systems itself; it reuses the registry from the Unicode CLDR project.
sections.plainLanguage: Your calendar file is written in one language of dates. Instead of rewriting it in another language, the repeat rule gets a note that says to count in a different calendar, and the program translates the answer back for you.

sections.title: How Instances Are Generated
sections.content:
The Gregorian calendar has 12 months, weeks of 7 days, and years of 365 or 366 days. The RECUR value in iCalendar has limits based on these facts, and other calendar systems differ, so this RFC leaves the maximum values for the RECUR elements to the calendar system in use.

Two principles apply. Calendar data keeps using the GREGORIAN calendar system, so all date and time values keep Gregorian format and limits. And RRULE gains an RSCALE element naming the calendar system for the pattern. Existing rules still hold, for example that the RRULE must match the DTSTART of the master instance, and properties such as RECURRENCE-ID, RDATE and EXDATE stay Gregorian.

The RFC suggests this procedure: convert the master component's DTSTART into the named calendar to get a seed; generate instances by applying the rule to the year, month and day there; then convert each instance back to Gregorian for use in other properties.
sections.plainLanguage: Translate the first date into the other calendar, count forward there the way the rule says, and translate every answer back so it fits on your normal calendar.

sections.title: The Extended RRULE Property
sections.content:
When RSCALE is present, RRULE changes in three ways. Numeric elements such as BYYEARDAY get ranges defined by the calendar system, since some systems have more than 366 days in a year. Month numbers may take an L suffix to mark a leap month. And a new SKIP element says how missing instances are handled.

The rscale value is either a registered calendar system name or an experimental x-name. Names are case insensitive, but uppercase is preferred. SKIP is one of OMIT, BACKWARD or FORWARD, defaults to OMIT, and MUST NOT be present unless RSCALE is.

Leap months are identified like this: numbers 1 through N name the regular months, and a leap month that follows a regular month gets that month's number plus L, so 5L follows the 5th regular month. The RFC warns about mapping to calendar libraries. The Hebrew calendar in ICU numbers months 1 through 13 with month 6 as the leap month, so ICU months 1 to 5 map to iCalendar 1 to 5, ICU month 6 maps to 5L, and ICU months 7 to 13 map to 6 to 12.

Valid RSCALE values come from the Unicode CLDR calendar registry, because many implementations will use the ICU library. CLDR aliases are allowed and treated as the calendar they point to. Agents SHOULD heed CLDR's deprecated and preferred values; for example islamicc is deprecated in favor of islamic-civil.
sections.plainLanguage: The repeat rule gets two new knobs: one picks which calendar to count in, the other says what to do on days that do not exist that year. Months that only appear in some years get a little L tag.

sections.title: Skipping Invalid Dates
sections.content:
In every calendar, some day and month combinations are invalid in a given year. A monthly event starting on January 31st hits months with fewer than 31 days, and February 29th does not exist in a non-leap year. RFC 5545 requires generators to ignore invalid dates, which can be surprising: someone born on a leap day would see their birthday only every four years. Humans usually expect a missing event to move to an earlier or later valid date.

SKIP offers three behaviors. OMIT is the default and ignores the invalid date, as before. BACKWARD changes an invalid month to the previous valid month and an invalid day to the previous valid day. FORWARD does the same toward the next valid month or day. If changing the month produces an invalid day, the skip is applied again for the day.

Skipping happens at set points in the BYxxx processing order: BYMONTH, then SKIP for an invalid month, then BYWEEKNO, BYYEARDAY, BYMONTHDAY, then SKIP for an invalid day, then BYDAY and the remaining elements. The RFC also notes that the real intent is often better encoded directly, for instance with BYMONTHDAY=-1 for the last day of every month.
sections.plainLanguage: If your birthday is on a day that some years do not have, you can choose: no party that year, party the day before, or party the day after.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC uses four examples. For Chinese New Year, DTSTART;VALUE=DATE:20130210 with RRULE:RSCALE=CHINESE;FREQ=YEARLY converts to the Chinese date {C}46500101, and adding one year at a time gives Gregorian dates 20140131, 20150219, 20160208 and 20170128. The {C}, {E} and {H} prefixes are only for illustration and never appear in real data.

For the first day of the Ethiopic 13th month, RSCALE=ETHIOPIC;FREQ=MONTHLY;BYMONTH=13 from 20130906 gives the same day in September each year, and shows a BYMONTH value above 12 that matches the Ethiopic month, not the Gregorian one.

A Hebrew anniversary on the 8th day of leap month 5L uses SKIP=FORWARD. Only year 5776 in the table is a leap year, so in other years the month moves forward to month 6. Finally, a Gregorian leap day (20120229) with RSCALE=GREGORIAN;FREQ=YEARLY;SKIP=FORWARD lands on the 1st of March in non-leap years, whereas without RSCALE it appears only in leap years such as 2016 and 2020.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show the idea in action: Chinese New Year lands on a different day on the wall calendar every year, and a leap-day birthday gets a party on March 1st in the years without a February 29th.

sections.title: Compatibility and iTIP
sections.content:
A calendar user agent that does not support RSCALE, or not the named calendar system, has three options: reject the whole iCalendar object, reject just the components that use it, or treat the component as non-recurring and effectively ignore the RRULE. Overridden components with the same UID MUST be rejected along with a rejected component, and SHOULD be rejected in the fall-back case. The RFC says option 2, rejecting just those components, is generally the best choice.

For iTIP (RFC 5546) scheduling messages, an agent without RSCALE support can reject the whole message with a REQUEST-STATUS of 3.1, or fall back to non-recurring behavior and reply with 2.3, 2.5, 2.8 or 2.10. An agent that supports RSCALE but not the named calendar SHOULD reject with 3.1. The RFC says rejecting the entire iTIP message is the best choice.
sections.plainLanguage: If a calendar app does not know the new rule, it should say no to just that one event instead of showing a wrong date, and keep the rest of your calendar working.

sections.title: xCal, jCal and CalDAV
sections.content:
For xCal (RFC 6321), the <recur> element gains child elements <rscale> and <skip>, each a string holding the RSCALE or SKIP value with case preserved, and <bymonth> may hold a number or a string. Appendix A updates the RELAX NG schema. For jCal (RFC 7265), the recur object gains rscale and skip string members, and bymonth is a number for plain integers but MUST be a string when the value has an L suffix.

For CalDAV (RFC 4791), servers need to support RSCALE because it determines the time ranges of recurring instances. A server advertises a CALDAV:supported-rscale-set WebDAV property, which MUST be protected and SHOULD NOT be returned by a PROPFIND allprop request, and which may list specific calendar systems in CALDAV:supported-rscale elements. If none are listed, clients can try any calendar and must expect possible failure. Clients MUST NOT store data containing RSCALE if the property is not advertised, and a server SHOULD answer an unsupported value with an HTTP 403 response containing a CALDAV:supported-rscale element. Existing clients are expected to fail gracefully by ignoring the component.
sections.plainLanguage: The same new rule has to be written down in the XML and JSON versions of calendars too, and a calendar server can post a sign saying which calendars it understands.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: This specification does not introduce any additional security concerns beyond those described in RFC 5545, RFC 5546 and RFC 4791.
sections.plainLanguage: The new rule adds no new dangers beyond the ones calendar programs already had.

items.label: Ignore
items.desc: Default. Ignore the invalid date, as in RFC 5545.

items.label: Move earlier
items.desc: Use the previous valid month or day.

items.label: Move later
items.desc: Use the next valid month or day.
